content:
Instances are exposed by default, presumably so we can unfold them to check they commute in various situations.

What exactly do we risk when we have a @[no_expose]d instance? When should we be careful about this? Is there a procedure for deciding that @[no_expose] is acceptable on an instance?

There are 2 risks we need to watch out for:

  • Diamonds. For example if you have a LE instance and a LinearOrder instance, you need to expose the last one of the two, and make sure that the LE field of the one unfolds to the other. That way, you know a ≤ b will always mean the same thing.
  • Proofs that were rfl might break. For example in ℝ, we have a - b defined as a + -b, and this instance is exposed, allowing rfl to rely on this. We could make the choice to not expose this if we want.

So re: diamonds, I suppose it's fair to say that if the class you're writing an instance of does not have any parent classes (assuming the correct direction of "parent"), you definitely do not need to worry about the first bullet! :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes: Or is there a"weird" way to create diamonds out of this situation?

There are some exceptions this, where we rely on some different defeq properties. For example, the nsmul/zsmul fields of a Ring need to be defeq to a general SMul instance if it exists (e.g. in MonoidAlgebra or Matrix), so that n • x always means the same.

Another interesting case is that some Algebra instance unifications rely on the fact that, for a : ℝ and b : ℂ, ↑a * b = a • b. To facilitate this defeq, but still expose as little as possible, I added docs#Complex.mulAux, which is not exposed, and is used to define both complex multiplication and complex scalar multiplication.
